lead: Four tests decide whether a series of positive terms converges, without adding infinitely many terms. Comparison places the series beside a known p-series. The integral test replaces the sum by an area. The ratio and root tests watch how fast terms shrink. These tools are used in probability, numerical error bounds and algorithm analysis. Only a few universities teach all four in one unit. This chapter keeps every term positive; signs come later.
prereq: You need: 3.1 and 3.2, limits from Unit 1, and improper integrals from Unit 2.

blocks.text: A series Σaₙ with aₙ > 0 for every n is a positive-term series. Its partial sums increase, so it either converges or tends to +∞. The p-series Σ 1/nᵖ converges exactly when p > 1 and diverges when p ≤ 1. Here p is a fixed real number and n starts at 1.
Direct comparison: if 0 ≤ aₙ ≤ bₙ for all large n, then Σbₙ convergent forces Σaₙ convergent; Σaₙ divergent forces Σbₙ divergent. The smaller series is squeezed under the larger.

Limit comparison: let bₙ > 0 and L = lim (aₙ/bₙ). If 0 < L < ∞, then Σaₙ and Σbₙ both converge or both diverge. If L = 0 and Σbₙ converges, then Σaₙ converges. If L = ∞ and Σbₙ diverges, then Σaₙ diverges. Choose bₙ as a simple p-series with the same growth. For example, aₙ = (2n+1)/(n³+5). For large n, aₙ behaves like 2n/n³ = 2/n². Take bₙ = 1/n². Then (aₙ/bₙ) → 2, and 0 < 2 < ∞. Since Σ1/n² converges (p=2>1), Σaₙ converges.

Let f be positive, continuous and decreasing on [1, ∞), and let aₙ = f(n). Then Σ_{n=1}∞ aₙ and ∫₁∞ f(x) dx both converge or both diverge. The sum is the area of rectangles of height f(n); the integral is the area under the curve. If the integral is finite, the rectangles fit under a finite area plus the first term. If the integral is infinite, the rectangles cover an infinite area.

items: Check that f(x) is positive, continuous and decreasing for x ≥ 1, where aₙ = f(n).
Take N → ∞. A finite limit means Σaₙ converges; an infinite limit means it diverges.

blocks.text: For Σ 1/n², take f(x)=1/x². It is positive, continuous and decreasing. ∫₁∞ x⁻² dx = [−1/x]₁∞ = 1, a finite number. So Σ1/n² converges. For a p-series, ∫₁∞ x⁻ᵖ dx is finite exactly when p > 1.

blocks.where: aₙ is the nth term of the series; L is the limit of the absolute ratio as n → ∞.

blocks.text: Ratio test: if L < 1, Σaₙ converges absolutely. If L > 1 (including L = ∞), it diverges. If L = 1, the test gives no conclusion. Factorials cancel in the ratio, so this test suits factorials and powers.
Root test: let L = lim |aₙ|^{1/n}. The same three rules hold. nth powers collapse under the nth root. Some syllabi call these D'Alembert's ratio test and Cauchy's root test.

Cauchy condensation: for a decreasing positive sequence, Σaₙ converges if and only if Σ2ⁿa_{2ⁿ} converges. This one-line variant handles series beyond p-series. For example, Σ1/(n log n) gives Σ2ⁿ/(2ⁿ log 2ⁿ) = (1/log 2)Σ1/n, which diverges, so Σ1/(n log n) diverges; the test also settles Σ1/(n(log n)²), which converges. When L = 1, switch to comparison or Raabe's test in 3.7. Do not call the series convergent.

figure.caption: The decision tree sends a positive-term series to one of four tests. Notice that factorials point to the ratio test and nth powers point to the root test.

spec.aria: A decision tree sends a positive series to the ratio test for factorials, the root test for nth powers, comparison for p-series shapes, and the integral test when an antiderivative is easy.

examples.question: Test the series Σ_{n=1}∞ n²/2ⁿ for convergence.
steps: The terms aₙ = n²/2ⁿ are positive for n ≥ 1.
Take the limit: as n → ∞, 1+1/n → 1, so L = 1²/2 = 1/2 = 0.5.
Since L = 0.5 < 1, the ratio test says the series converges.
examples.answer: The series Σ n²/2ⁿ converges; the ratio limit is 1/2.

traps: If the ratio or root test gives L = 1, it gives no information. Do not write convergent; use comparison or Raabe's test.
In direct comparison, a series larger than a divergent series diverges; a series smaller than a convergent series converges. The other two directions fail.
The p-series Σ1/nᵖ diverges at p = 1 and converges for every p > 1, even p = 1.0001. Check the exponent, not the number of terms.
The integral test needs f decreasing. A positive continuous f that rises first may break the rectangle comparison.
Limit comparison needs 0 < L < ∞. If L = 0 or L = ∞, only one direction follows.

quiz.q: State the convergence condition for the p-series Σ1/nᵖ.
quiz.a: Σ1/nᵖ converges if p > 1 and diverges if p ≤ 1.

quiz.q: Why does L = 1 in the ratio test give no conclusion?
quiz.a: Both convergent and divergent series can give L = 1, for example Σ1/n² converges and Σ1/n diverges.
Take bₙ = 1/n² > 0. Then aₙ/bₙ = (n+1)n²/(n³+2) = (n³+n²)/(n³+2) → 1, so L = 1 and 0 < L < ∞. Both series behave alike. Since Σ1/n² converges (p-series with p = 2 > 1), Σ (n+1)/(n³+2) converges.

quiz.q: Use the root test on Σ (n/(2n+1))ⁿ.
quiz.a: L = lim n/(2n+1) = 1/2. Since L = 1/2 < 1, the series converges.

quiz.q: List the three conditions on f for the integral test.
quiz.a: f must be positive, continuous and decreasing on [1, ∞), with aₙ = f(n).
Use the ratio test. L = lim (n+1)/10 = ∞ > 1, so the series diverges.

beyond: Not for the exam. The integral test gives error bounds for numerical sums, because the tail sits between two integrals. The ratio test appears in generating functions and in convergence of power series. The root test is a standard tool in analytic combinatorics. The p-series with p = s is the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) = Σ1/nˢ for real s > 1. Search next for Cauchy condensation test, ratio test error bound, and Riemann zeta function.
